stem:
Mehak's science diary follows a solar calendar of 365 days most years. She reads that Earth takes nearly 365.25 days to revolve around the Sun, so an extra day is added every fourth year.

Why do solar calendars use that leap-day adjustment?

options.text: The extra quarter-days add up to about one full day every four years, so a leap day keeps the calendar aligned with the seasons.
Solar calendars add a leap day because the Moon completes twelve exact months in 365 days.
Solar calendars stay aligned with the seasons even if the extra quarter-days are never corrected.
A leap day is added so that the seasons first create the extra quarter-days of Earth's revolution.

teacher.key_rationale: Earth's ~365.25-day year leaves quarter-days that total about one day every four years; a leap day keeps the solar calendar with the seasons. Blaming the Moon swaps the idea; skipping the correction omits the needed adjustment; putting seasons as the cause of the quarter-days reverses the relationship.
